title: UNIT 5: CHEMICAL EQUILIBRIUM
notes:
✓ Chemical equilibrium → Deals with reversible chemical reactions that can proceed in both forward and reverse directions.

At equilibrium, the forward and reverse reactions continue simultaneously at equal rates, so the macroscopic concentrations of reactants and products remain constant.
✓ Equilibrium is dynamic, not static.

title: 5.1 Introduction
notes:
Some chemical reactions proceed almost completely to products, while others do not. In reversible reactions, products can react again to form the original reactants.

Chemical equilibrium explains why a reversible reaction does not necessarily go to completion, how equilibrium is established, how much reactant and product is present at equilibrium, and how changes in conditions affect the equilibrium position.

✓ A chemical system must be able to undergo both forward and reverse reactions for dynamic equilibrium to be established.

title: 5.2 Chemical Equilibrium
notes:
✓ Chemical equilibrium → The state reached by a reversible reaction when the rate of the forward reaction becomes equal to the rate of the reverse reaction.

For a general reaction:
aA + bB ⇌ cC + dD

✓ At equilibrium → Rate of forward reaction = Rate of reverse reaction.

The concentrations of reactants and products remain constant with time, although the particles continue to react at the microscopic level.

✓ Equilibrium does not mean that the concentrations of reactants and products are equal.

title: 5.2.1 Reversible and Irreversible Reactions
notes:
◆ IRREVERSIBLE REACTION
✓ A reaction that proceeds mainly in one direction and approaches completion.
→ Represented by a single arrow (→).

◆ EXAMPLE
C(s) + O₂(g) → CO₂(g)

◆ REVERSIBLE REACTION
✓ A reaction in which products can react to form the original reactants.
→ Represented by a double arrow (⇌).

General form:
aA + bB ⇌ cC + dD

→ Forward reaction forms products, while the reverse reaction converts products back into reactants.

◆ EXAMPLE
N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g)

title: 5.2.2 Attainment and Characteristics of Chemical Equilibrium
notes:
Consider:
N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g)

At the beginning, the forward reaction is fast because the reactant concentrations are high, while the reverse reaction is very slow because little or no product is present.

As the reaction proceeds, reactants decrease and products increase. Therefore, the forward rate decreases while the reverse rate increases. Eventually the two rates become equal and equilibrium is established.

◆ CHARACTERISTICS OF EQUILIBRIUM
✓ It is dynamic.
✓ Forward and reverse reactions continue.
✓ Forward and reverse rates are equal.
✓ Concentrations remain constant.
✓ Reactant and product concentrations are not necessarily equal.
✓ A closed system is required for equilibrium to be maintained.

title: 5.2.3 Conditions for Attainment of Chemical Equilibrium
notes:
◆ CONDITIONS
✓ The reaction must be reversible.
✓ The system should be closed so that reactants and products cannot continuously escape.
✓ Temperature must remain constant while a particular equilibrium constant is being considered.
✓ Sufficient time must be allowed for the forward and reverse reaction rates to become equal.

Once equilibrium is reached, macroscopic properties such as concentration, pressure, and other measurable properties remain constant with time, provided the external conditions are unchanged.

title: 5.2.4 Equilibrium Expression and Equilibrium Constant
notes:
✓ Equilibrium constant → Expresses the relationship between the concentrations or partial pressures of products and reactants at equilibrium.

For:
aA + bB ⇌ cC + dD

✓ Kc = [C]ᶜ[D]ᵈ / [A]ᵃ[B]ᵇ

→ The coefficients in the balanced equation become the powers in the equilibrium expression.

✓ The equilibrium constant has a fixed value for a particular reaction at a particular temperature.

title: 5.2.4.1 Meaning of the Equilibrium Constant
notes:
The magnitude of K gives an indication of the relative amounts of products and reactants at equilibrium.

✓ Kc > 1 → Products are favored at equilibrium.
✓ Kc < 1 → Reactants are favored at equilibrium.
✓ Kc ≈ 1 → Significant amounts of both reactants and products are present.

✓ A large K does not mean that the reaction is fast.
→ Equilibrium constant describes equilibrium composition, not reaction rate.

title: 5.2.4.2 Homogeneous and Heterogeneous Equilibrium
notes:
◆ HOMOGENEOUS EQUILIBRIUM
✓ All reactants and products are in the same physical state.

◆ EXAMPLE
H₂(g) + I₂(g) ⇌ 2HI(g)

◆ HETEROGENEOUS EQUILIBRIUM
✓ Reactants and products occur in more than one physical state.

◆ EXAMPLE
CaCO₃(s) ⇌ CaO(s) + CO₂(g)

✓ Pure solids and pure liquids are not included in the equilibrium constant expression because their concentrations remain effectively constant at a given temperature.

For the reaction above:
✓ Kc = [CO₂]

title: 5.2.4.3 Equilibrium Constant in Terms of Partial Pressure
notes:
For gaseous equilibrium systems, equilibrium can be expressed using partial pressures.

For:
aA(g) + bB(g) ⇌ cC(g) + dD(g)

✓ Kp = (Pᴄ)ᶜ(Pᴅ)ᵈ / (Pᴬ)ᵃ(Pᴮ)ᵇ

where P represents the equilibrium partial pressure of each gas.

✓ Kp = Kc(RT)ᵟⁿ

where:
✓ Δn = Total moles of gaseous products − Total moles of gaseous reactants.

→ Only gaseous species are considered when calculating Δn.

title: 5.2.5 Applications of the Equilibrium Constant
notes:
The equilibrium constant can be used to calculate unknown equilibrium concentrations or partial pressures and to determine whether products or reactants are favored.

◆ CALCULATION STEPS
✓ Write and balance the equilibrium equation.
✓ Write the correct Kc or Kp expression.
✓ Substitute the known equilibrium values.
✓ Solve for the unknown quantity.

When the initial concentrations and Kc are known, an equilibrium table can be used to determine the change in concentration and the final equilibrium concentrations.

→ The equilibrium constant also allows comparison of the relative amounts of reactants and products at equilibrium.

title: 5.2.5.1 Reaction Quotient
notes:
✓ Reaction quotient (Q) → Has the same mathematical form as the equilibrium constant but can be calculated using concentrations or partial pressures at any stage of the reaction, not only at equilibrium.

For:
aA + bB ⇌ cC + dD

✓ Qc = [C]ᶜ[D]ᵈ / [A]ᵃ[B]ᵇ

◆ COMPARING Q WITH K
✓ Q < K → Reaction proceeds in the forward direction to form more products.
✓ Q > K → Reaction proceeds in the reverse direction to form more reactants.
✓ Q = K → System is at equilibrium.

title: 5.2.5.2 Predicting the Direction of a Reaction
notes:
The relationship between Q and K predicts the direction in which a reaction must proceed to reach equilibrium.

✓ Q < K → Relatively too few products are present → Reaction shifts toward products.
✓ Q > K → Relatively too many products are present → Reaction shifts toward reactants.
✓ Q = K → Reaction mixture is already at equilibrium → No net shift.

title: 5.2.6 Le Chatelier’s Principle
notes:
✓ Le Chatelier’s principle → When a change is imposed on a system at equilibrium, the equilibrium position shifts in the direction that tends to reduce the effect of that change.

◆ MAJOR CHANGES
✓ Concentration.
✓ Pressure or volume.
✓ Temperature.

→ The system responds to the disturbance and establishes a new equilibrium.

title: 5.2.6.1 Effect of Concentration
notes:
✓ Increasing the concentration of a reactant → Equilibrium generally shifts toward products to consume some of the added reactant.
✓ Increasing the concentration of a product → Equilibrium shifts toward reactants.
✓ Removing a reactant → Equilibrium shifts toward reactants.
✓ Removing a product → Equilibrium shifts toward products.

◆ EXAMPLE
N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃

→ Adding N₂ shifts the equilibrium to the right.
→ Removing NH₃ also shifts the equilibrium to the right.

title: 5.2.6.2 Effect of Pressure and Volume
notes:
Pressure changes significantly affect equilibria involving gases.

✓ Increasing pressure by decreasing volume → Equilibrium shifts toward the side with fewer moles of gas.
✓ Decreasing pressure by increasing volume → Equilibrium shifts toward the side with more moles of gas.
✓ Equal total moles of gaseous species on both sides → Pressure or volume change does not shift the equilibrium.

◆ EXAMPLE
N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g)

Left side → 4 moles of gas.
Right side → 2 moles of gas.

✓ Increasing pressure → Favors NH₃ formation.

title: 5.2.6.3 Effect of Temperature
notes:
✓ Temperature changes affect both the equilibrium position and the value of the equilibrium constant.

◆ EXOTHERMIC FORWARD REACTION
Reactants ⇌ Products + heat

✓ Temperature ↑ → Equilibrium shifts toward reactants.
✓ Temperature ↓ → Equilibrium favors products.

◆ ENDOTHERMIC FORWARD REACTION
Reactants + heat ⇌ Products

✓ Temperature ↑ → Equilibrium favors products.
✓ Temperature ↓ → Equilibrium favors reactants.

✓ Temperature is the only common equilibrium condition that changes the value of K.

title: 5.2.6.4 Effect of a Catalyst on Equilibrium
notes:
A catalyst increases the rates of both the forward and reverse reactions by providing a lower-energy pathway.

◆ A CATALYST DOES NOT
✓ Shift the equilibrium position.
✓ Change the equilibrium concentrations.
✓ Change the value of K.

✓ A catalyst only helps the system reach equilibrium more quickly.

→ A catalyst changes the rate at which equilibrium is reached, but not the final equilibrium composition.

title: 5.2.6.5 Effect of Changes on K
notes:
✓ The equilibrium constant K depends on temperature.

Changing concentration or pressure changes the equilibrium position but does not change K at a fixed temperature.

Adding a catalyst also does not change K.

◆ EXOTHERMIC REACTION
✓ Temperature ↑ → K generally decreases.
✓ Temperature ↓ → K generally increases.

◆ ENDOTHERMIC REACTION
✓ Temperature ↑ → K generally increases.
✓ Temperature ↓ → K generally decreases.

title: 5.2.7 Equilibrium and Industry
notes:
Industrial chemical processes are designed to obtain useful products at practical rates and acceptable yields. Le Chatelier’s principle is used to choose suitable temperature, pressure, concentration, and other operating conditions.

◆ INDUSTRIAL APPLICATIONS
✓ Haber process → Ammonia production.
✓ Contact process → Sulfuric acid production.

title: 5.2.7.1 Haber Process — Ammonia
notes:
The Haber process manufactures ammonia from nitrogen and hydrogen:

N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g) + heat

✓ The forward reaction is exothermic.

◆ EFFECT OF CONDITIONS
✓ High pressure → Favors NH₃ because the product side has fewer gas molecules.
✓ Low temperature → Favors NH₃ because the forward reaction is exothermic.
✓ Very low temperature → Makes the reaction too slow.
✓ Iron catalyst → Increases reaction rate without changing the equilibrium position.

The industrial process uses a compromise of approximately 200–400 atm and about 500 °C.

→ Ammonia is continuously removed by cooling and liquefying it, while unreacted nitrogen and hydrogen are recycled.

title: 5.2.7.2 Contact Process — Sulfuric Acid
notes:
The Contact process is used to manufacture sulfuric acid, H₂SO₄. An important reversible step is the catalytic oxidation of sulfur dioxide:

2SO₂(g) + O₂(g) ⇌ 2SO₃(g) + heat

✓ The reaction is exothermic.

◆ MAIN STEPS
◆ 1. Production of sulfur dioxide
S + O₂ → SO₂

◆ 2. Oxidation of SO₂ to SO₃
2SO₂ + O₂ ⇌ 2SO₃
✓ Catalyst → V₂O₅
✓ Temperature → About 450 °C

◆ 3. Formation of oleum
SO₃ + H₂SO₄ → H₂S₂O₇

◆ 4. Formation of sulfuric acid
H₂S₂O₇ + H₂O → 2H₂SO₄

→ The temperature and pressure are selected as compromises between equilibrium yield and reaction rate.

title: UNIT 5 — MUST REMEMBER
notes:
✓ CHEMICAL EQUILIBRIUM → State in which the forward and reverse reaction rates are equal.
✓ DYNAMIC EQUILIBRIUM → Forward and reverse reactions continue even though macroscopic concentrations remain constant.
✓ REVERSIBLE → Reaction proceeds in both directions and is represented by ⇌.
✓ IRREVERSIBLE → Reaction proceeds mainly in one direction and is represented by →.

✓ Kc → Equilibrium constant based on concentrations.
✓ Kp → Equilibrium constant based on partial pressures of gases.
✓ GENERAL Kc → Kc = [C]ᶜ[D]ᵈ/[A]ᵃ[B]ᵇ.
✓ Kp → Kp = (Pᴄ)ᶜ(Pᴅ)ᵈ/(Pᴬ)ᵃ(Pᴮ)ᵇ.
✓ Kp = Kc(RT)^Δn.
✓ HETEROGENEOUS EQUILIBRIUM → Pure solids and pure liquids are omitted from K expressions.

✓ K > 1 → Products favored.
✓ K < 1 → Reactants favored.
✓ Q < K → Reaction moves forward.
✓ Q > K → Reaction moves backward.
✓ Q = K → Equilibrium.

✓ LE CHATELIER → An equilibrium shifts to oppose an imposed change.
✓ CONCENTRATION ↑ → Equilibrium shifts away from the added substance.
✓ PRESSURE ↑ → Gas equilibrium shifts toward fewer gaseous moles.
✓ TEMPERATURE ↑ → Favors the endothermic direction.
✓ CATALYST → Speeds up both directions equally; does not change K or equilibrium position.

✓ HABER PROCESS → N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃; used to manufacture ammonia.
✓ CONTACT PROCESS → 2SO₂ + O₂ ⇌ 2SO₃; important step in sulfuric acid manufacture.

✓ KEY IDEA → Equilibrium is not a stopping point. It is a dynamic state where forward and reverse processes continue at equal rates.
